rationale: Start with a broad, moderately fast scouting gradient to locate the elution window and critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Raise temperature while keeping the gradient fixed to test selectivity in the crowded middle cluster. The current elution window is comfortably below 10 minutes, so resolving the critical pair is the priority.

Use a shallower gradient at the better-performing temperature to improve resolution of the remaining critical pair. The current last peak at 6.49 minutes leaves room to increase separation while targeting elution within 10 minutes.

The shallower gradient improved the neighboring separations but worsened the critical pair, indicating a selectivity limitation. Raise temperature by 5 C to shift that pair apart while retaining the extra separation around it and keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.
The maximum CRF is achieved; now shorten the gradient by one grid step to seek a faster fully resolved method. Monitor both close pairs, retaining injection 4 as the proven fallback.

Lower the starting organic fraction to test whether altered gradient selectivity can restore the newly limiting pair at the shorter gradient duration. Injection 4 remains the fully resolved, maximum-score fallback.

With a maximum-score method secured, test a cooler, faster gradient for an alternative selectivity window. Lower temperature may separate the middle cluster differently, potentially allowing full resolution at a shorter elution time.

Test a hot, fast gradient for a different selectivity window, potentially after an elution-order crossover in the middle cluster. The maximum-score methods remain secured while this run probes substantially shorter analysis time.

Test a higher starting organic fraction with a moderately shallower gradient to redistribute spacing within the hot-gradient middle cluster. This probes a faster selectivity window while retaining injection 6 as the shortest proven fully resolved method.

Test whether the lower starting organic fraction preserves the middle-pair spacing at 50 C while a steeper gradient improves the other critical separation. This targets full resolution substantially faster than the proven 7.60-minute elution window.

Probe the cooler side of the middle-cluster selectivity crossover using the original gradient. This tests whether the critical pair separates in the opposite elution order without the extensive co-elution seen at 25 C.

Refine around injection 6 with a slightly steeper slope, using a lower endpoint to obtain a smaller slope change than shortening tG alone. This tests whether full resolution can be retained with an earlier last peak.

Combine a higher starting organic fraction with a shallower slope to preserve the limiting middle-pair separation while reducing initial retention. This tests whether a shifted gradient window can beat injection 6's 7.60-minute fully resolved elution time.

Test whether a shallower gradient at 40 C resolves the critical cluster on the opposite side of its temperature-dependent crossover. The higher starting organic fraction should offset some of the added retention while keeping the early pair separated.
Shorten the newly fully resolved 40 C method by one grid step to locate its speed limit. Monitor the middle cluster, particularly the pair that had only R = 1.58 at 16 minutes.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to shorten retention while slightly reducing gradient slope, which may restore the limiting middle-pair resolution. Check the early pair as well, since higher starting organic can compress its separation.

Refine the near-successful injection 5 by slightly lowering the endpoint, making the gradient shallower without adding programmed gradient time. This should improve its R = 1.29 pair and may retain full resolution near the shortest proven elution time.

Use a slope between injections 4 and 17 to bring the R = 1.47 pair above threshold while preserving the other critical separation. The endpoint remains above the organic fraction at which the last peak eluted in those runs, so truncation is unlikely.

Test whether a shallower gradient at 60 C moves the temperature-sensitive middle pair beyond its crossover into full resolution. The hotter column should keep the last peak near or below 10 minutes, with the established maximum-score methods retained as fallbacks.

Return to the shortest proven fully resolved method and lower the endpoint one step to test resolution robustness. This slightly shallower gradient should improve the close earlier pair, while checking whether the later pair retains its narrow margin above R = 1.5.

Refine the successful 55 C region with a slope between injections 4 and 18, seeking more balanced margins for the two critical pairs. This should retain maximum CRF with the last peak near 8 minutes; injection 6 remains the fastest proven fully resolved method.

Shorten the programmed gradient while preserving injection 6's successful slope of 0.075 organic fraction per minute. Its last peak eluted before this new gradient would finish at the outlet, so full resolution and the 7.60-minute elution window should be retained.

Raise the endpoint one step from injection 22 to test the speed boundary of the shortest proven fully resolved method. The steeper slope should advance the last peak, but the middle pair at R = 1.59 may become limiting.

Lengthen injection 13's gradient one step to restore its limiting pair while targeting stronger resolution margins than the fastest method. Injection 22 remains the preferred speed benchmark, with maximum CRF and all peaks eluted by 7.60 minutes.

Lower injection 24's endpoint one step to improve its remaining R = 1.41 pair, targeting full resolution with the last peak still below 10 minutes. This final refinement seeks greater resolution margins; injection 22 remains the shortest proven maximum-score method.
